You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The failing test `testCodec98NPE` writes a 1024-byte buffer (codec98_1024) to a `Base64OutputStream` with decoding mode (doEncode=false). In `Base64OutputStream.write(byte[], int, int)` method, this triggers `base64.decode(b, offset, len)`.

Inspecting the `Base64.decode(byte[], int, int)` method reveals that if inAvail (the length of input) is negative, the `eof` flag is set to true (line 555). The method loops over input bytes, making sure to allocate/resize the buffer via `resizeBuffer()` if buffer is null or too small. Iteration updates `modulus` and `x` to collect 4 Base64 chars before decoding to bytes into buffer.

At end of method, if eof is true and modulus != 0, final bytes are added to the buffer corresponding to the leftover bits. The buffer, which must have been initialized or resized earlier, is accessed here.

The `resizeBuffer()` method initializes the `buffer` when null by allocating a default sized byte array.

The crux of the current NPE bug from the report is that under certain input conditions, the `buffer` stays null when `Base64.decode` is called with inAvail = -1 (EOF condition). This leads to a NullPointerException when the final bytes are written to the buffer since `buffer[pos++] = ...` attempts to access null.

Looking at the test, close() method in `Base64OutputStream` calls `base64.decode(singleByte, 0, -1)` (lines 188-193). This sends EOF with a negative length at the end of stream.

The test inputs trigger a code path where `buffer` has not been initialized (likely because `resizeBuffer()` was never called or buffer null check is insufficient) before reaching the final EOF processing block.

Hence the bug happens because EOF input (inAvail = -1) triggers decode(), but buffer is still null leading to NullPointerException at line 591 and following where buffer[pos++] is accessed.

Recent bug reports do not seem directly related to this NPE or decode buffer initialization.

This strongly indicates a missed initialization or resizeBuffer call for buffer when inAvail < 0 (EOF) in decode(), or a faulty condition checking initialization of buffer before writing leftover decoded bytes on EOF.

Recommended fix might be to ensure buffer initialized when decode is called with EOF (-1 length) and modulus != 0 or to add a guard null check before buffer usage at the end.

Thus, the root cause of NPE is that `Base64.decode()` assumes buffer has been initialized by resizeBuffer() during the byte-processing loop, but if inAvail < 0 (EOF) is passed directly without other bytes processed, buffer remains null and leads to crash when writing final decoded bytes.

Final diagnosis: The NullPointerException in the failing test is caused by `Base64.decode()` method being called with a negative inAvail (EOF) before any buffer allocation occurs, resulting in `buffer` being null when final decoded bytes are accessed.

This matches exactly the summary and description of the current bug report.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
